count-charge-and-isotopes: Check which particles are counted in the mass number A. Did either of the departing particles come from the nucleus?
What number identifies an element on the periodic table? Did losing electrons change that number?
translate-an-energy-scale: In the photon rule, energy times wavelength has a fixed value. Check whether that product would stay fixed.
Try increasing both the energy and the wavelength. Would their product match the original one?
read-a-spectral-gap: Move both marks on an energy ladder up by ten units. What happens to the distance between the marks?
The two levels still have a gap. What would need to happen to that gap for the photon energy to vanish?
binding-needs-a-reference: Think of the zero level as the top of a pit. Which starting level needs a bigger lift to get out?
Locate the new level relative to the zero-energy boundary. Is it above the edge of the pit yet?
label-hydrogen-states: Start the allowed orbital labels at zero and stop one step below n. Which choices appear on that list?
Write the integer labels from zero through n minus one. Which proposed label falls outside your list?
a-shell-is-not-an-orbit: Picture a spherical shell shrinking toward a point. How does the area of the shell change as its radius shrinks?
The question asks about one thin shell at a particular radius. How does that differ from the volume of the whole atom?
subtract-hydrogen-energies: Use the energy at each end of the transition. Does a larger level number alone tell you the size of the gap?
Plot the first three energies using the inverse square of n. Are the marks equally spaced?
allowed-does-not-mean-certain: A selection rule checks whether a transition can occur. What else would you need to predict its waiting time?
Could two allowed pairs of states overlap by different amounts? What might that do to their transition rates?
two-kinds-of-angular-momentum: The length of an angular-momentum arrow and its vertical component have different allowed values. List the allowed m labels.
The symbol L describes orbital angular momentum. Which measurement would include the spin as well?
couple-spin-to-orbital-motion: Find the smallest and largest j using the difference and the sum of l and s. How far apart are those bounds?
The positive and negative signs can label projections. Are you counting projections or total j values?
split-levels-with-a-field: Compare two products with the same factors except for the sign of one factor. What happens to the size of the product?
Look for the signed quantity in the shift formula. Does fixing the magnetic field also fix that sign?
resolve-smaller-structure: Check what Z counts. Which smaller splitting can depend on a nuclear property even if Z stays fixed?
An electron can interact with the nucleus's magnetic moment. Which energy splitting would respond to that interaction?
fill-states-not-locations: For each spatial orbital, draw a place for each of the possible spin directions. Then count all the places.
How many spin choices does one electron have per spatial orbital? Multiply that number by the number of orbitals.
screen-the-nuclear-pull: Imagine moving closer to the nucleus than most of the screening charge. How much of the nuclear pull gets through?
Screening describes where the electrons are. Did the number of protons physically change?
use-filling-to-explain-trends: Count positive and negative charges before and after the outer electron leaves. Do they still balance?
Mark the departing electron on a before-and-after sketch. Which particles stayed inside?
an-average-field-misses-correlations: Which differences between energy levels are tested by that one line? What other states or properties could you measure?
Try picturing two approximate energies with the same error. How could their difference still match the measured line?
light-can-drive-either-direction: A population tells you how many atoms occupy each level. Does moving atoms between levels change their nuclei?
The gap between the two energy levels stays fixed. What changes when more atoms occupy the upper level?
lifetime-predicts-a-population-curve: Use the survival factor for one mean lifetime and apply it twice. Is a mean lifetime the same as a half-life?
Sketch an exponentially falling curve. Does it reach the axis after two finite steps?
a-line-has-a-shape: Check whether lifetime multiplies or divides the constant in the natural line-width rule.
Imagine observing the wave for a longer time. How would that affect how precisely its frequency is defined?
gain-needs-a-supplied-energy-source: Follow the light over one trip around the cavity. Where does energy lost at a mirror go?
Start with a small light pulse and compare its strength after both amplification and loss on one round trip.
a-molecular-well-has-a-minimum: Place a marble on a hilltop and give it a tiny nudge. Does the force bring it back?
Sketch both a valley and a hill. Which point is deep enough to hold a slightly disturbed marble?
separate-fast-and-slow-motion: The separation of fast and slow motion relies on a clear separation of electronic energies. What changes near a crossing?
Two energy surfaces approaching each other concerns how motions affect one another. Did the nuclear charges change?
read-rotational-and-vibrational-spacings: Put J equal to one and two in the rotational energy formula. Are the two resulting energies equal?
List the first three values of J times J plus one. Compare the steps between them.
zero-point-energy-reduces-dissociation-e: Mark the dissociation threshold and both starting levels on the same energy ladder. Which starting point is closer?
Keep the breakup threshold fixed and measure upward from each possible starting level. Is the distance the same?
identify-a-nucleus: Which label counts only protons, and which includes both protons and neutrons?
Mark the extra neutron inside the nucleus. Which total includes that new particle?
nuclei-grow-by-volume: Sketch spheres holding different numbers of particles at the same density. Can both spheres keep the same radius?
The particle count scales with volume. Which root converts a volume factor to a radius factor?
mass-difference-stores-binding: Write the free mass first and subtract the bound mass. What sign is possible for this hypothetical ordering?
Recall the conversion between mass and energy. What does multiplying a signed mass difference by that factor give?
compare-binding-per-nucleon: An average is per nucleon. What total would you get by multiplying each average by its own nucleon count?
Compare the products of each binding per nucleon and its particle count. What would be required for equal totals?
nuclear-attraction-is-short-ranged: Compare a nearby pair of nucleons with a widely separated pair. Which force in this question depends on short distances?
Sketch a small group and a large group. Would a particle near one edge be equally close to every other particle?
balance-liquid-drop-contributions: Find the sign in front of the electrical penalty in the binding expression. What happens when that term grows?
Keep every other term fixed and change only the penalty in the binding calculation. Which term could offset it?
shell-gaps-matter-in-nuclei: Converting units rescales every energy. Would that single out one particular particle count for extra stability?
Think about filling a set of states up to a gap. What would it cost to put the next nucleon above the gap?
spin-and-parity-test-a-model: Parity describes what a wave does when you reverse the coordinates. What separate comparison tells you whether the state is bound?
Look at what receives the minus sign under reflection. Is that quantity the energy or the wave amplitude?
random-decays-smooth-average: Picture a single nucleus before and after bringing a second independent sample nearby. Did its individual decay rule change?
Each original sample had some expected decays in a minute. How would combining their counts make those events disappear?
half-life-is-not-mean-lifetime: Start with one whole sample and apply the same halving step three times. How do repeated halvings combine?
Try the same steps starting with eighty nuclei on average. Does the expected count ever reach zero in those steps?
activity-is-a-rate: Imagine splitting a sample into two equal parts and counting just one part. How many potential decays are you watching?
Use activity as the number of nuclei times the individual decay rate. Which factor became smaller?
a-daughter-can-also-decay: Imagine water flowing into and out of a bucket at equal rates. What stays steady while water is still flowing?
Does balancing the arrival and removal of daughter nuclei change the properties of an individual daughter?
alpha-decay-crosses-a-barrier: Subtracting particle labels identifies the daughter. Which information would give a probability per unit time?
Compare two nuclei with different barriers. Which feature could change how often an alpha particle gets through?
beta-decay-shares-energy: List the particles already present in beta-minus decay before proposing an extra charged particle. Does the proposed list balance charge?
Trace the energy of every product, including the moving daughter. How much can you infer from the electron alone?
gamma-emission-includes-recoil: At fixed photon energy the recoil momentum is fixed. Where does the nuclear mass appear in kinetic energy at fixed momentum?
A photon of the same nonzero energy carries momentum away. What must the recoiling nucleus carry?
conservation-filters-decay-stories: Write a separate energy budget after checking charge. What energy is available from a parent initially at rest?
Compare the total energy before and after. What could supply the extra product rest energy in this setup?
charged-particles-leave-energy-behind: A unit tells you how a quantity is measured. What evidence would show that its value stays constant as the particle slows?
Compare the beginning and end of a particle's track. Why might energy loss per unit distance differ?
attenuation-removes-unscattered-photons: Which directions and kinds of photons did the narrow detector count? Compare that with the wider detector's tally.
Draw a photon changing direction on a collision. Could it still reach a detector covering a wider angle?
separate-efficiency-and-background: Imagine sending the same number of events to a detector that now catches a smaller fraction. Which way would its count change?
Separate the events produced from those recorded. Which number does efficiency describe?
count-uncertainty-survives-subtraction: Imagine repeating both counts tomorrow. Would subtracting a background reading make the two random changes match?
What range of counts might appear if you repeated just the background measurement several times?
balance-reaction-labels: Matching charge and nucleon counts is one check. Which quantities would you compare to tell whether energy is released?
Even if a neutron is captured, which measurements of the starting and ending particles give the energy balance?
q-measures-rest-energy-change: Think of a reaction whose incoming particles carry kinetic energy. What could that energy help pay for?
A negative Q means the final rest energy costs extra. Trace where the extra energy could come from.
cross-section-turns-flux-into-rate: Flux counts incoming particles. Did the number of particles already in the target change?
Distinguish how many particles arrive from the chance of an interaction per target particle. Which did you change?
threshold-needs-momentum-room: Draw the incoming momentum arrow. Could all final particles be at rest in this laboratory frame?
At the threshold, the products still have to carry the initial momentum. What might this require in addition to their rest energy?
rearrangement-can-release-binding-energy: Place the initial and final rest energies on a ladder. Which side must supply energy when the final level is higher?
Count rest energy alongside motion and radiation. What quantity must still balance across the rearrangement?
a-chain-is-a-causal-sequence: Releasing energy describes the first event. What observation would tell you whether a later event followed from it?
A produced neutron has several possible outcomes. What would you need to know before predicting the next event?
fusion-faces-electric-repulsion: Draw the energy at the start, at close approach, and at the finish. Which comparison does positive Q describe?
Picture two positively charged particles approaching slowly. What could turn them away before they touch?
stars-couple-nuclear-physics-to-transpor: Imagine a warm object that keeps shining after its heater is turned down. What supplies the difference for a while?
Consider the hot gas inside the star. Which quantity in its energy budget can fall while light escapes?
infer-an-original-spectral-ladder: Shift all three levels up by the same amount. What happens to each possible difference between levels?
List each pair of the three levels once and subtract their energies. Which gaps are actually available?
fit-a-decay-record-cautiously: Use a separate detection fraction for each time in the ratio of recorded counts. Do the two fractions cancel?
Compare a drop in true activity with a drop in detection efficiency. Which of them could lower the later count?
balance-and-test-a-synthetic-reaction: Q compares energies. Which separate quantity would tell you how frequently the channel occurs?
The energy budget is defined before any detector sees the products. What instrument property sets the fraction recorded?
compare-the-models: Compare the size and pattern of the mismatch with the measurement uncertainty. Which input could you check independently?
Could carrying more digits correct a wrong input value or a physical effect left out of the model?
